titulo: Safety and efficacy of feed additives consisting of tinctures derived from the roots or leaves and stems of Althaea officinalis L.: Marsh mallow root tincture for use in all animal species and marsh mallow leaf tincture for use in horses and dogs (FEFANA…
extracto: Following a request from the European Commission, EFSA was asked to deliver a scientific opinion on the safety and efficacy of two tinctures obtained from the roots (marsh mallow root tincture) or leaves and stems (marsh mallow leaf tincture) of Althaea officinalis L. when used as sensory additives. The additives are water/ethanol tinctures, with a specified dry matter content of 2%–3% (w/w) (marsh mallow root tincture) and not more than 25% (w/w) (marsh mallow leaf tincture). Marsh mallow root tincture is intended for use in feed or water for drinking for all animal species, while marsh mallow leaf tincture is proposed for use in feed for horses and dogs. The EFSA Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed (FEEDAP) concluded that marsh mallow root tincture is safe at the maximum proposed use level of 250 mg/kg complete feed for all animal species. Marsh mallow leaf tincture is safe at the maximum proposed use level of 1000 mg/kg complete feed for horses and 325 mg/kg complete feed for dogs. No safety concern would arise for the consumer and the environment from the use of marsh mallow tinctures in animal feed. The additives under assessment should be considered as irritant to skin and eyes, and as dermal and respiratory sensitisers. Exposure of users by any route is considered a risk. Since the roots of A. officinalis are recognised to flavour food and their function in feed would be essentially the same as that in food, no further demonstration of efficacy for marsh mallow root tincture was considered necessary. The same conclusions are extended to marsh mallow leaf tincture.

titulo: Model development to predict environmental concentrations of chemical substances in marine sediment when the substance is applied via feed in marine aquaculture: Task 3.1a, Plan the pilot web application
extracto: The present report outlines the planning and deployment of a pilot web application designed to provide a user‐friendly, browser‐based interface for running a coupled hydrodynamic–sediment–chemical dispersion model that predicts Predicted Environmental Concentrations (PEC) of feed additives in marine sediments beneath sea‐cage aquaculture. The application will support the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA's) tiered environmental risk assessment by allowing non‐programmers to configure key model parameters, automatically selecting between precomputed lookup‐table outputs or full numerical model reruns depending on user inputs. Built in open‐source languages and deployable via the European Digital Twin for the Ocean (EDITO) Kubernetes‐based cloud infrastructure, the app will integrate a modular architecture with a front‐end dashboard, a queue manager, and a computational back‐end capable of overnight simulations for step II scenarios. Drawing on a representative set of European aquaculture sites and precomputed 3‐D hydrodynamic results, the system will deliver PEC values and uncertainty estimates, with additional diagnostics for full model runs.

titulo: Assessment of guanidinoacetic acid (GAA) and a preparation of GAA (Creamino®) as feed additives for chickens for fattening and reared for breeding/laying, weaned piglets and pigs for fattening, for the renewal of their authorisation and its extension of…
extracto: Following a request from the European Commission, EFSA was asked to deliver a scientific opinion on the feed additives guanidinoacetic acid (GAA) and a preparation of GAA (Creamino®) for chickens for fattening and reared for laying and breeding, weaned piglets and pigs for fattening for the renewal of their authorisation and their extension of use in feed for suckling pigs. The additives are already authorised for use in chickens for fattening and reared for laying and breeding, weaned piglets and pigs for fattening. The FEEDAP Panel concludes that the additives remain safe for the target species, consumers and environment and that the extension of the use to suckling piglets would not affect these conclusions. Regarding user safety, the additives were not considered irritant to skin or eyes and were not considered a potential skin sensitiser. There is no need for assessing the efficacy of the additives in the context of the renewal of the authorisation for chickens for fattening, chickens reared for laying and breeding, weaned piglets and pigs for fattening. The Panel concludes that the additives are efficacious in feed for suckling piglets at 600 mg/kg complete feed.

titulo: Scoping review of existing in silico and PBK models for humans and rats
extracto: One of EFSA research priority research areas is to better understand the role of toxicokinetic and its implementation into next generation risk assessment. Food ingredients and contaminants often lack data on their absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME) properties, which are needed to model their bioavailability using Physiologically Based Kinetic (PBK) models. The project ADME4NGRA, “Implementing the EFSA NAMs roadmap through advancing toxicokinetic knowledge in chemical risk assessment”, aims to provide a list of NAM‐based ADME tools and guidance for parameterising PBK models for rats and humans. The first step (and aim of this report) is to characterise the landscape of available in silico models, in vitro‐in vivo extrapolation (IVIVE) methodologies and PBK models. The results of a scoping review and the assessment of currently available generic PBK platforms as well as newly developed and existing in silico models are herein reported and discussed, highlighting knowledge and data gaps relevant for the assessment of compounds occurring in food and feed.

titulo: Update of the risk assessment on dioxins and dioxin-like PCBs in feed and food
extracto: The European Commission asked EFSA to update its 2018 risk assessment on polychlorinated dibenzo‐p‐dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/Fs) and dioxin‐like polychlorinated biphenyls (DL‐PCBs) in feed and food, based on the 2022 WHO Toxic Equivalency Factors (WHO 2022 ‐TEFs). A decrease in sperm concentrations as a consequence of early‐life exposure was still considered the critical effect in rodents and humans. This can only be prevented by ensuring sufficiently low exposure to PCDD/Fs and DL‐PCBs of future mothers. Using the WHO 2022 ‐TEFs, the critical human study in the 2018 Opinion still showed a significant inverse association between PCDD/Fs and sperm concentration, but not when including DL‐PCBs. Therefore, this study was not used to derive a Tolerable Weekly intake (TWI). Instead, a developmental study with TCDD in rats was used to derive a TWI of 0.6 pg. WHO 2022 ‐toxic equivalents (TEQ)/kg bw per week, based on decreased sperm production. Human studies were used as supporting evidence, including an evaluation of necessary uncertainty factors. Dietary exposure assessment based on occurrence data in food from the last decade, showed that using the new TEFs resulted in 27%–35% lower total‐TEQ exposure. Mean exposure (lower to upper bound) to PCDD/Fs and DL‐PCBs for European adult populations varied between 1.87 and 6.10 pg. WHO 2022 ‐TEQ/kg bw per week, and at the P95 between 4.15 and 12.0 pg. WHO 2022 ‐TEQ/kg bw per week. The CONTAM Panel concluded that exposure for European women of childbearing age raises a health concern for their sons at the mean (80%–90% certainty) and P95 (95%–99% certainty) exposure. Including uncertainties regarding the TEFs for DL‐PCBs decreased this certainty. Human milk data confirmed the exceedance of the TWI but to a lesser extent than dietary exposure. The change in TEFs does not affect the transfer rates of individual congeners but it could impact the transfer rates when using Total‐TEQ levels.

titulo: Model development to predict environmental concentrations of chemical substances in marine sediment when the substance is applied via feed in marine aquaculture: Task 1.4. Model setup and analysis
extracto: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assesses the safety of fish feed additives used in aquaculture. To evaluate their potential environmental risks, it is essential to calculate the predicted environmental concentrations (PEC) and compare them to known exposure thresholds. This report outlines the setup and analysis of a model established in earlier phases of the project to get it functioning with default data and parameter sets, and to explore its sensitivity and applicability. The model is configured using environmental input data (derived from large‐scale ocean and atmosphere models across Europe) and applies standardised parameter sets representing the most common finfish aquaculture species (salmon, sea bass, and sea bream). It is implemented within a containerised system, ensuring portability and ease of deployment across computing environments. The automated modelling pipeline is broadly applicable, although performance can be challenged in areas with complex bathymetry; in these cases, targeted adjustments to default settings and workflow configurations have been explored. Model results indicate that predicted environmental concentrations (PECs) are sensitive to specific parameters, particularly those governing sediment consolidation and additive mixing depth. These parameters should therefore be prioritised in future calibration and validation efforts. The approach adopts high‐resolution, process‐based modelling across a range of representative environmental conditions to derive PEC estimates. Compared with more simplified (idealised) modelling approaches, this framework better reflects real‐world conditions, enables direct comparison with site‐specific observations, and produces outputs that are more readily interpretable for end users and decision‐makers. However, these advantages come with practical challenges, including the need to ensure robust automation across diverse environmental settings and the potential for bias in the selection of representative sites.
